Our releases happen in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets stay in place after the switch.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest is what browsers use to find assets. As soon as it changes, browsers start requesting the new names. If the manifest switched before the upload finished, those requests would hit files that don't exist yet, and the page would break. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when it goes live. Versioned names make this safe: the new files can't overwrite anything the current release is using, so uploading them has no effect on live traffic until the switch.

**Why we keep the old assets:** A browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the old names for the rest of that session. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would get missing scripts, styles, or images partway through their visit. Keeping the old assets lets each browser finish with a consistent set of files from whichever release it started on.

Each release has two steps. First we upload every new asset under a versioned name. Then we switch the manifest so it points to those names. We never overwrite or delete the previous release's assets as part of the release.

**Why upload comes first:** The manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it before the new files existed, any browser that fetched the new manifest in that gap would request files that aren't there. The result is broken pages, missing styles, or scripts that fail. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the manifest goes live. The switch is then a single change from one complete release to another.

**Why we keep old assets:** Browsers don't all move to the new release at the same moment. Someone who loaded the page a minute before the switch still has the old manifest. As they navigate or lazy-load code, they'll keep requesting the old versioned files. If those files were gone, that user's session would break partway through, even though nothing was wrong with either release. Leaving the old assets available lets in-flight sessions finish on the release they started with. New page loads pick up the new manifest naturally.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. Because new files never reuse an old name, uploading them can't disturb the live release, and old and new can coexist without either one overwriting the other.

Our static-site releases happen in two steps: we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets stay where they are.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest switch is the moment browsers start asking for the new names. If we switched before the upload finished, a browser could fetch the new manifest and then request an asset that doesn't exist yet. The result would be a broken page. Because the assets are already in place before the switch, every name the new manifest points to resolves from the first request.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the page before the switch is still working from the previous manifest. It will keep requesting the old versioned names as it loads scripts, styles or images. If we deleted those files at release time, those users would hit missing assets mid-session. Keeping the old assets lets those browsers finish on the version they started with, while new visitors get the new one.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so the old and new releases can be served side by side, and the manifest switch is the only thing that decides which release a browser uses.

Here's how a release works and why the steps are in this order.

When we release, we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so a new build never overwrites a file from the current one. Once everything is uploaded, we switch the manifest to point at the new names. That switch is the moment the release goes live.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest tells browsers which files to request. If we switched it before the uploads finished, any browser that fetched the new manifest would ask for files that don't exist yet and get errors, so the page would load broken. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when the manifest goes live. Until then, browsers keep using the old manifest and old files, which are untouched. Nobody sees a half-finished release.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already have the previous one, such as open tabs or pages loaded just before the release. Those browsers keep requesting the old names, for example when they load a file they hadn't needed yet. If we deleted the old assets, those requests would fail and the page would break for those users. Versioned names let both releases sit side by side without conflict. New visitors get the new files, and existing sessions keep working with the old ones.
